html:
The Lisbon earthquake struck on the morning of 1 November 1755, All Saints' Day. With the tsunami and fires that followed, it almost completely destroyed Lisbon, the capital of Portugal, and killed tens of thousands of people.

The quake, centred in the Atlantic south west of Portugal, is now thought to have been around magnitude 8.5 or more. It came while many people were at Mass, and churches collapsed on them. Survivors fled to the open waterfront, where a tsunami struck about forty minutes later. Candles and kitchen fires then started blazes that burned for days. The waves also hit Morocco and southern Spain.

The response:

  • The king's chief minister, later the Marquis of Pombal, took charge. He is said to have ordered: bury the dead and feed the living.
  • Lisbon's lower town was rebuilt on a grid, with buildings on a wooden frame designed to flex in a quake, among the first such codes anywhere.
  • Pombal sent a questionnaire to every parish about what they had felt and seen, which makes the quake one of the first studied scientifically.

The disaster shook European thought. Why would a good God destroy a Catholic city on a holy day? Voltaire wrote a poem on it and mocked the belief that all is for the best in Candide. Rousseau answered that people, not nature, had chosen to crowd into tall buildings. Kant wrote essays on the causes of earthquakes. It is often seen as a turning point in Enlightenment faith in a kindly ordered world.
sum: The Lisbon earthquake struck on the morning of 1 November 1755, All Saints' Day. With the tsunami and fires that followed, it almost completely destroyed Lisbon, the capital of Portugal, and killed tens of thousands of people.
